answer: Each agent holds a signed lantern token from a trusted registrar; to act it must publish the token’s hash to an echo pool that timestamps it on a public ledger. The pool checks the hash against a jetty of historic issuance records, rejecting any token that does not echo a known chain. An attacker therefore must recreate the full issuance history for each fake identity, paying the cumulative registration fees and computational work, which scales linearly with the number of Sybil nodes.
